name: english_03
context: An English tweet from the SemEval-2017 sentiment analysis dataset. The tweets were found by searching Twitter for popular topics of the time, such as public figures, products, places, events and political issues, and were posted between 2012 and early 2017. At least five crowd workers labelled the overall sentiment of each tweet.

versions.analysis_for_next: Trimmed version 1 to fit the 400-word limit. The fixes are the same as before. Event promos, invitations, ticket sales and plans to attend are now neutral, since annotators labelled most of these neutral. Calm analytical or argumentative opinions and tense news without casualties are now neutral too. Negative needs explicit negative emotion, personal inconvenience or harmful news. Positive includes good news such as wins, records and desirable launches.

Version 1 overcorrected. Positive recall fell from 164 to 112, with 76 positive texts predicted neutral. Annotators often label positive when there is any warmth, even without strong emotion words. Examples:
- friendly invitations: 'come see me!!', 'See you there!', 'Hope to see you then'
- good-luck wishes
- plans the author looks forward to: 'Guess who's going to see Foo Fighters', 'going to Disneyland'
- holiday fun: 'National Ice Cream Day', 'Star Wars DAY'
- new product, release or tour news: Apple event, Plan B tour
- tributes to dead stars: George Harrison, Wilt Chamberlain

The neutral texts that annotators keep neutral are dry logistics and ads, bare ticket sales, questions, and analytic opinions.

Middle ground for version 2:
- Positive covers any warmth, anticipation, well-wishing, tribute, or good or new-product news.
- Neutral covers dry information, scheduling, commercial ads, questions, speculation and analysis.
- Negative stays as in version 1, which worked reasonably. It needs explicit annoyance, insults, disappointment, or harm.
- Mild self-deprecating stress, hypothetical sadness and ironic exaggeration stay neutral.
- Tributes and RIP posts lean positive, not negative.
next_examples_not_copied: It’s Tuesday night in Athens! AKA karaoke night at the Volstead so come see me!!

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 2 is the best so far at 72.4. Positive recall recovered, but 49 neutral texts are still predicted positive. Most are hype-style promos and invitations ('come party with us', 'OMG who wants to go see Duelo', 'Looks like BJ's Skate Center is the place to be'), fandom rambles, and news recaps containing 'win' or 'crush'. Annotators keep these neutral when the author states no personal feeling. I'll say that hype phrasing, exclamation marks and party promotion alone do not make a tweet positive.

Negative to neutral has 43 errors, and two kinds stand out:
- Personal setbacks marked by #fml, 'crying', :((((, 'the tragedy of', or gallows jokes.
- News of trouble, such as charges, investigations, scandals, 'problems for', or being close to war.

I'll add both to negative, along with critical rhetorical questions aimed at a politician or institution.

The neutral texts predicted negative are mostly sports takes, mock-dramatic fandom posts and stressed-but-joking posts. I'll keep these neutral with a clearer example.

RIP posts are mixed: praise or tribute is positive, but 'sad that he died' is negative.

Version 3's new line, that hype and party promos without a personal feeling are neutral, cost too much positive recall. Positive fell from 166 to 130, and 62 positive texts were predicted neutral. Annotators give positive to upbeat promos ('come see me!!', 'See you there!'), exciting release or tour news, wins, holiday posts ('Star Wars DAY!') and fun personal plans. The neutral to positive errors it fixed were fewer than the positive errors it caused.

So version 4 returns to version 2's positive definition, the best at 72.4. It keeps version 3's sharper negative cues for personal setbacks and trouble news, which held negative recall steady. To limit neutral to positive errors, I keep only the narrow case: bare logistics, ads and ticket listings, and plans stated with no upbeat tone, are neutral. Calm sports and political takes, mock-dramatic fandom posts and joking stress stay neutral.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 4 (71.3) came out slightly below version 2 (72.4). Its line that bare listings and promos are neutral, together with the extra negative examples, lowered positive recall (166 to 154) without cutting neutral-to-positive errors (51 against 49). Most remaining errors look like label noise. Examples:
- Similar enthusiastic invitations are labelled positive in one tweet and neutral in another.
- Sports critiques are labelled negative in one tweet and neutral in another.

So version 5 goes back to version 2's wording, the best performer, with small safe changes:
- Add personal-setback markers (#fml, crying) as negative cues only, not as examples.
- Add excited fan outbursts (OMG, flailing, all caps) to the positive cues, since several positive fan tweets were missed.
- Keep version 2's neutral examples, which anchor promos without warmth, calm sports takes and hypothetical sadness.
next_examples_not_copied: It’s Tuesday night in Athens! AKA karaoke night at the Volstead so come see me!!

versions.analysis_for_next: Same as version 6, trimmed to fit the word limit. Plain or hedged plans and activity reports are neutral, in contrast with excited plans, which are positive. The Paper Towns example replaces the promo example. Everything else follows version 5, the best so far.
next_examples_not_copied: It’s Tuesday night in Athens! AKA karaoke night at the Volstead so come see me!!

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 6 (71.9) scored below version 5 (72.8). Calling plain plans neutral moved some neutral texts out of positive, but it cost more positive recall (167 to 155). Plans stay as in version 5.

Version 7 is version 5 with one targeted change on the negative side. About 37 to 42 negative texts are still predicted neutral, and many of them are news of trouble: manslaughter charge, under investigation, 'Problems for Newcastle', close to war, punished in scandal. Version 4, which had a charge-news negative example, reached the highest negative recall (148). That version's positive losses came from its 'dry listings' line, not from the negative example.

So I'll swap the obvious Sharknado example for the Caitlyn Jenner charge example. I'll also add charge, scandal, investigation and problems to the negative rule and cues. Positive and neutral wording stays exactly as in version 5.

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 7 is the best so far at 73.6. The trouble-news negative example raised negative recall to 150 without hurting positive (166).

The remaining systematic leak is neutral texts predicted negative (29). Most are blunt opinions about athletes, politicians or groups that use no emotion words. Examples: 'dustin johnson ... folds up like a lawnchair', 'progressives pretty much stop at the border', 'I thought Christians followed Christ', 'Mariners fall ... Another tough pen day', 'Josh Hamilton ... just looks at it. Lol'. Annotators treat these as opinion or commentary, not feeling.

The current neutral anchor (Pochettino) is a mild take. I'll swap it for a harsher sports take that annotators still called neutral, and name blunt sports and political critiques in the rule. Negative keeps explicit anger or insult words and trouble news.

Neutral to positive (50) looks mostly like noise, since enthusiastic invitations are labelled both ways. The positive side stays unchanged.
next_examples_not_copied: It’s Tuesday night in Athens! AKA karaoke night at the Volstead so come see me!!

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 8 (73.2) scored slightly below version 7 (73.6). Anchoring neutral with a harsh sports critique cut neutral-to-negative errors (29 to 22), but more true negatives slipped to neutral (30 to 39). Negative recall fell from 150 to 141.

Annotators often do treat critical commentary as negative, so version 9 returns to version 7's structure: the milder Pochettino neutral anchor, and the trouble-news negative example.

The only change is to the negative cues: sarcastic pity ('feel sorry for'), 'meltdown' and 'not happy'. These appeared in missed negatives and are unlikely to pull neutral texts over. Positive and neutral wording stay as in version 7, which gave the best balance.
next_examples_not_copied: It’s Tuesday night in Athens! AKA karaoke night at the Volstead so come see me!!

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 9 (73.1) changed only the negative cues from version 7 (73.6) and scored slightly lower, so the added cues did not help. The remaining errors are mostly ambiguous or inconsistently labelled tweets:
- enthusiastic invitations labelled both positive and neutral
- sports critiques labelled both neutral and negative
- product and rumor news labelled positive

Earlier attempts to shift these boundaries each traded one confusion for another:
- calling plans neutral (version 6)
- calling hype neutral (version 3)
- calling blunt critiques neutral (version 8)
- calling dry listings neutral (version 4)

For the final version I return to version 7 exactly, the best-balanced definition. Positive covers broad mild warmth plus good-news and product announcements. Neutral covers dry information, ads, questions and calm analysis. Negative covers explicit negative emotion, personal setbacks, and news of harm or trouble, anchored by a charge-news example.
